::: {.callout-note}
## Scoped, not yet run
:::

## The question

@Morozov_2021 gives the cleanest statement of why preferences and search costs
are separable: stopping decisions depend on the *realized* utilities of
alternatives already searched but not on their search costs, which are sunk.
Trade the utility intercept against the search cost so as to hold the mean
reservation value fixed and the search *order* is unchanged — but the higher
intercept raises realized utility and makes stopping more likely.

His Appendix D turns this into an observable moment: the **recall rate**, the
probability of buying an alternative encountered earlier in the sequence rather
than the most recent one, responds to the intercept but not to the search cost.

**Ask:** does the recall rate actually move that way in SIFT data, and is it
sharp enough at realistic task counts to be worth reporting as a diagnostic?

## Design

1. Two sweeps holding the mean reservation value fixed: one varying the utility
   intercept, one varying the search-cost intercept.
2. Compute the recall rate directly from the click sequence — no model.
3. Check that it responds to the first sweep and not the second, and estimate
   how many tasks are needed to detect the difference.

SIFT observes recall directly, because respondents have free recall and we
record the entire sequence, so this needs no modelling assumption at all.

## The second, harder question

@Morozov_2021 proves nonparametric identification of individual-level
preferences *and* search costs from panel search data, but the argument takes
the number of sessions per consumer to infinity; with a mean of 5 he estimates
hyperparameters rather than individual parameters.

**Ask:** at $T \in \{4, 8, 16, 32\}$, how close do individual-level posteriors
get to the truth, and where does the hierarchical prior stop doing most of the
work? This is the number that tells a practitioner how many tasks to field, and
it is the honest version of the claim that the panel buys individual-level
estimates.
